questions.q: What does a secure view hide that an ordinary view does not?
options: The row data returned by the view
The view's own SQL definition, from anyone without the privilege to see it
The name of the view itself
The warehouse used to query the view
questions.explain: By default, a view's SELECT statement is visible via SHOW VIEWS or GET_DDL even to those who can't query the underlying table. SECURE hides that definition from anyone without the right privilege.

questions.q: What is the exact syntax difference between creating a regular view and a secure view?
options: CREATE SECURE VIEW instead of CREATE VIEW — everything else about the definition stays the same
Secure views require a separate ROW ACCESS POLICY object
Secure views can only be created by the PUBLIC role
Secure views must be created inside the ACCOUNT_USAGE schema
questions.explain: The only syntax change is CREATE SECURE VIEW in place of CREATE VIEW; the SELECT statement and everything else about defining the view stays identical.

questions.q: What does the IS_SECURE column, returned by SHOW VIEWS, tell you?
options: Whether the view has ever been queried
Whether the view is currently marked SECURE, without needing to re-read its full definition
How many roles have access to the view
Whether the view references a masked column
questions.explain: SHOW VIEWS reports IS_SECURE as TRUE or FALSE, letting you confirm a view's secure status at a glance rather than inspecting its full SQL definition.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does a secure view give up in exchange for hiding its definition?
options: Nothing — there is no trade-off
The ability to be queried by any role
Some query optimizer visibility, such as predicate pushdown across the view boundary, which can mean fewer available execution-plan optimizations
The ability to reference more than one base table
questions.explain: A secure view's query isn't exposed to the optimizer the same way a regular view's is, which can limit certain optimizations like predicate pushdown — a real reason not to make every view secure by default.

questions.q: Which of these is a good candidate for SECURE, per this lesson?
options: A one-off internal view with no sensitive logic, queried only by trusted admins
A multi-tenant view like widgets_view, where the WHERE clause logic and referenced table names shouldn't be exposed to every querying role
A view that never changes and has no WHERE clause at all
Any view, since SECURE should always be the default
questions.explain: Good candidates include views wrapping row access or masking logic, views handed to external/shared consumers, and multi-tenant views like widgets_view — not every view by default, given the optimizer trade-off.
